hints: Start at the top of the tree - what is constantly being lost from the leaves, and what does that loss do to the water status in the leaf cells?
Think about how water molecules interact with each other through their polarity - what kind of bond holds one water molecule to the next?
Now think about how water molecules interact with the walls of the narrow xylem vessels as well as with each other - why does the whole column stay intact?
Link the pull from above to the movement below - what name is given to this pulling force, and what gradient does it create from roots to leaves?
walkthrough:
Start With The Engine - Transpiration In The Leaves**
Leaves are constantly losing water vapour by transpiration through open stomata. Losing water lowers the water potential of the mesophyll and leaf cells, so they draw water from the xylem in the leaf veins. That creates a difference in water potential between the top and bottom of the tree.

Pull The Rope - Transpiration Pull And Continuous Columns**
Because xylem vessels form hollow, continuous tubes from roots to leaves, the pull at the top is transmitted all the way down. Water is pulled up as an unbroken column. We call this transpiration pull, part of the cohesion-tension mechanism. It is a pull, not a push from the roots, so avoid saying water is pushed up.

Why The Column Does Not Snap - Cohesion**
Water is polar, so water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other. This attraction between water molecules is cohesion. It gives the water column high tensile strength, so when the top molecules are pulled up, the molecules below are dragged up with them without the column breaking, even in a tall trunk.

Why Water Clings To The Sides - Adhesion**
Water molecules also form hydrogen bonds with the walls of the xylem vessels. This is adhesion to cellulose in the walls and to hydrophilic parts of lignin. Adhesion helps the column stick to the sides and move up by capillary-like support, working together with cohesion to maintain upward flow.

Final answer: Water moves up as a continuous column in xylem vessels down a water potential gradient, driven by transpiration pull via cohesion-tension. Evaporation from leaves lowers leaf water potential, pulling water up. Cohesion by hydrogen bonding between water molecules keeps the column intact, and adhesion by hydrogen bonding to xylem walls / cellulose / lignin supports upward movement.

walkthrough:
Link Cavitation To Daytime Water Flow**
Remember the stem tells you cavitation forms more often when water moves fast in xylem. Fast movement means high transpiration. In Fig. 3.1, clicks are only recorded when photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) is above zero, i.e. in daylight when stomata are open for photosynthesis and transpiration occurs. At night when PAR is zero, cavitation rate falls to zero.

Spot That It Is Not A Simple Proportional Relationship**
A good conclusion also says what is not seen. Although cavitation needs light, a higher PAR value does not always give a higher cavitation rate. The peaks of cavitation do not coincide exactly with the peaks of PAR or wind speed. So you cannot claim a clear positive correlation between PAR intensity and number of clicks.

Compare Light And Wind**
Now compare like with like for the two factors. Cavitation stops when wind speed falls below about $1.25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, but even with wind present, cavitation still needs light. Overall, PAR affects cavitation / water movement more strongly than wind speed does, because presence or absence of light switches cavitation on or off.

Final answer: Cavitation / rapid water movement only occurs when PAR / light is present for photosynthesis / transpiration, with zero cavitation at night. There is no clear proportional relationship between PAR value and cavitation rate and peaks do not coincide exactly with peaks in PAR or wind speed. No cavitation occurs when wind speed is below about $1.25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, and PAR has a greater effect on cavitation than wind speed.
